title: Kathina, deeper
hookLine: cloth offered, a robe cut and sewn by the community within a day

cards: Late evening at a monastery in Myanmar. In a hall lit with bulbs, teams of young women sit at wooden looms, racing. They've been weaving since the night before.
By dawn, the robes must be woven, finished and offered, and crowds come to cheer them on. It's a contest, and also something older: a gift that must be made in a single stretch of time.
You met Kathina in your first year: the thirty monks in muddy robes at the end of the rains, and the Buddha's allowance of new cloth. Today, inside the ceremony itself.

teach.b: Kathina has a few rules that make it unlike any other gift. First, timing: it can be held only in the month after the rains retreat ends, and only at a monastery where monks have completed the retreat.
Second, the cloth must be offered freely. Monks can't ask for it, hint at it, or arrange it.
Lay people bring it, unasked, to the whole community, not to one monk. Third, the community decides.
In a formal act, the monks agree together to give the cloth to one of their number, often someone whose robes are worn or who is respected for his conduct.
The fourth rule is today's line: the robe must be made that very day.
The old texts describe cloth washed, measured, cut, sewn, dyed and finished before dawn, with the whole community helping.

In some places today the cloth arrives already made, and the community completes the formal act the same day. The Myanmar weaving contest, held on an autumn full moon, carries the old urgency in a new form.
Why a single day? The texts don't explain. Some teachers point to what it does: it gathers everyone at once, lay and monastic, around one task no one person can do alone.
The robe that comes out is ordinary cloth. What's special is the night everyone spent making it together.

how: In Theravada communities, lay people bring Kathina cloth and other gifts to a monastery in the month after the rains; the monks formally give the cloth to one of their number, and in Myanmar some temples hold overnight robe-weaving contests.

games.q: you're a monk. the Kathina cloth has come, and the community chooses you. it's afternoon. what must happen?
o: take the cloth to a tailor next week.
make the robe that day, with the community's help.
keep the cloth as it is.
games.why: in the old practice, the robe was washed, cut, sewn and dyed before dawn, with everyone helping.

practice: Picture a piece of cloth in your hands with a loose button or a small tear, and the needle going in and out, slowly, each stitch a breath. Notice how mending asks for patience: you can't rush a stitch.
If sewing isn't for you, picture one small thing in your home that needs repair, and fixing it carefully.

wordCard.voice: Kathina. The cloth offering after the rains: given unasked, given to one monk by the community's choice, and made into a robe in a single day. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali kathina: firm, hard; thought to refer to the wooden frame used for sewing robes.

carryVoice: Your line: sewn in a day. Many hands, one night, one robe. Day six hundred eighty-nine, done.
